query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small controlled amount of Al to a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating promotes formation of a protective oxide scale at elevated temperatures, thereby reducing wear and microscopic deformation during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a conventional metal substrate (undoped).
generation.intervention: Co-sputter the coating with a precisely controlled Al fraction (e.g., up to a few atomic percent).
generation.conditions: High-temperature tribological tests (e.g., pin-on-disk) at 600–800 °C under fixed load and sliding speed.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable Al-rich oxide surface layer under the sliding contact.
generation.mechanism: The Al-rich oxide film serves as a protective barrier at high temperatures, decreasing abrasive contact and inhibiting severe plastic deformation in the subsurface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced wear rates and smaller deformation zones for Al-doped coatings, relative to the undoped baseline, in the 600–800 °C sliding regime.
generation.baseline: Undoped FeNiCrCoCu coating of the same thickness tested under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: Effects should be observed within moderate Al doping levels at 600–800 °C; extrapolation outside this doping range or temperature window remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Though similar Al-containing high-entropy coatings have shown improved high-temperature wear performance, direct confirmation for FeNiCrCoCu with Al doping is not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Deposit both undoped and Al-doped FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates, then perform side-by-side elevated-temperature sliding wear tests.
measurements: Measure coating mass loss or thickness reduction to quantify wear.
Characterize wear track surface and subsurface by SEM/EDS/XRD to check for oxide scale formation and deformation features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped coating shows no significant improvement in wear resistance or microstructural stability relative to the baseline, or no Al-rich oxide layer forms under the specified conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . chosen.lever: Al doping fraction in FeNiCrCoCu coating
chosen.technique: Co-sputtering to vary Al content and high-temperature tribological testing (e.g., pin-on-disk)
chosen.conditions: Sliding at 600–800 °C under controlled normal load and velocity
chosen.why: By introducing a small, precisely controlled Al fraction into the FeNiCrCoCu system, the hypothesis is that Al-driven oxide formation at high temperatures is the key mechanism governing both wear resistance and microstructural stability under sliding. Prior studies of HEAs and conventional alloys indicate that controlled Al additions promote the formation of robust, lubricious oxide scales, reduce friction, and mitigate sliding-induced plastic deformation. The new baseline condition is the as-deposited, undoped FeNiCrCoCu coating, from which the Al-doped variant is systematically compared. The hypothesis predicts that higher Al doping should yield (i) reduced wear rates and (ii) reduced microscopic deformation in the high-temperature sliding regime, consistent with protective oxide layer formation. A result that would falsify this mechanism is failure to observe improved wear performance or any corresponding stable oxide scale on the Al-doped coatings relative to the undoped baseline under the same high-temperature sliding conditions.
